before: Missing forwarding evidence can reflect packet loss, contention or an unobserved transmission, making feedback design a joint problem of inference and airtime. We benchmark ACK-gated censored passive feedback against active proofs in 750 IEEE 802.15.4 runs on 30 new fixtures, with naive-passive, frozen-prior and capacity-matched policy controls. Under blackholes, delivery increases from 71.28% to 75.94%, a paired gain of 4.67 percentage points (95% interval 2.36–6.97; Holm-adjusted p=0.0161). Energy per delivered byte falls while total modeled radio energy rises slightly. The controls do not establish a unique censoring or attention advantage. A separate 180-run experiment tests frozen policies over authenticated messages and node-local records. Attention delivers 81.61% in benign conditions and 61.11% under selective dropping, without an established advantage over greedy or multilayer-perceptron routing. Serial-interface testing identifies and corrects a receive-time freshness error. Compiled UART-to-radio firmware runs on four emulated Cortex-M3 boards; neural inference and cryptography execute on the host PC. Each host-policy control delivers ten of ten packets. An exploratory 60–300 s extension exposes routing-energy exhaustion and increasing service debt. The contribution is a traceable comparison of feedback mechanisms and transport boundaries; the evidence does not establish sustained operation, physical-board performance, measured energy consumption or absolute deadline compliance.

before: A four-second horizon, a central sink and a 60-packet burst are insufficient to establish steady-state scalability or network lifetime. After cache sorting, candidate scoring is linear in the bounded candidate count. Record expiry is more costly: each millisecond poll scans all W retained watches, giving O(W) work and O(W) memory. The experiments provide neither a long-horizon reclamation policy nor measured embedded inference cost. An always-listening radio also omits the wake-up cost that evidence collection would incur under duty cycling.

before: ACK-gated censored passive feedback passed the prespecified replacement test on 30 new fixtures, improving blackhole delivery over active proofs by 4.67 percentage points. The matched controls establish neither a unique censoring effect nor an attention advantage. In the separate 180-run authenticated transport study, frozen policies operate on received wire state and local service records without an established attention benefit. Serial-interface testing corrected a receive-time error, and four emulated Cortex-M3 boards execute the compiled UART-to-radio bridge while inference and cryptography remain on the host. The 60–300 s extension exposes routing-energy exhaustion and increasing source debt. Together, these results define the benchmark’s supported feedback comparison and deployment boundary: absolute service compliance, physical-board operation, embedded policy/crypto execution and measured energy remain unvalidated.

before: The 150 ms evidence timeout includes contention, retries and forwarding. Interference can therefore delay a valid receipt past expiry. Censoring avoids assigning failure solely from silence and allows a later receipt to upgrade the record; it does not establish an optimal timeout. The simulator also uses a shared time base. The corrected host timestamp sampling error is different from device clock offset or drift, which remain untested.

before: A useful next step is to decide when forwarding evidence is worth collecting. An observation policy could choose silence, passive listening or an authenticated probe according to the expected reduction in delivery loss relative to measured radio and processing cost. A discriminating experiment would match feedback semantics and data airtime, introduce duty cycling and adversarial receipts, and reserve new topologies and physical-board settings. This would test evidence acquisition itself, which the current comparison cannot isolate.
after: Section 5.6 separates proof generation from the declared evidence rule, but its periodic sleep primitive lacks rendezvous. An observation policy could choose silence, passive listening or an authenticated probe according to the expected reduction in delivery loss relative to measured radio and processing cost. A discriminating deployment experiment would integrate rendezvous, test adversarial receipts and clock uncertainty, and reserve new physical-board settings. This would evaluate evidence acquisition under execution costs absent from the isolated harness.

before: The action and ledger audit checked 67,522 decisions, 24,747 passive observations, 28,353 evidence updates and 75,750 node-energy identities. A separate endpoint audit reconstructed delivery and critical-violation values for all 750 runs from source decision times and sink receptions, then checked beacon counts, decision counts and PHY-state energy. All 30 gzip streams were read to completion. The original-stage suite had 51 passing tests; the expanded implementation now has 83 passing tests, including the radio callback checks.
